<div class="fs-kicker">TMUA · Paper 2 · Mathematical Reasoning · Arg3, Arg4</div>
<div class="fs-title">Quantifiers & Negation — Key Concepts</div>
<div class="fs-sub">Two quantifiers — <strong>for all</strong> and <strong>there exists</strong> — and the rules for negating any statement built from them. The three moves that do everything: <em>flip the quantifier &amp; negate the inside</em>, <em>De Morgan on and/or</em>, and <em>negate an implication as "hypothesis and not conclusion"</em>. And watch the <strong>order</strong> of two quantifiers — it changes the meaning.</div>
::::

## Quantifiers and their negations

:::: {.fs-grid}

::: {.fs-card}
### For all / there exists

**for all** — a claim about **every** object. **there exists** (= **for some** = **for at least one**) —
a claim that **at least one** object works.

$$\text{"for some"} = \text{"there exists at least one"}$$

[a "there exists" is **false** only when *nothing* works; a "for all" is **false** as soon as *one* thing
fails]{.eg}
:::

::: {.fs-card}
### The two negation rules

$$\text{not}(\text{for all } x,\ P)=\text{there exists } x,\ \text{not }P$$
$$\text{not}(\text{there exists } x,\ P)=\text{for all } x,\ \text{not }P$$

**Flip the quantifier *and* negate the inside — both, every time.**

[changing only one of the two is the single commonest error on this topic]{.eg}
:::

::: {.fs-card}
### De Morgan — negating *and* / *or*

$$\text{not}(A \text{ and } B)=(\text{not }A)\ \textbf{or}\ (\text{not }B)$$
$$\text{not}(A \text{ or } B)=(\text{not }A)\ \textbf{and}\ (\text{not }B)$$

Negating swaps **and ↔ or**.

[not("$n$ odd **and** $n>100$") $=$ "$n$ even **or** $n\le100$"]{.eg}
:::

::: {.fs-card}
### Negating an implication

$$\text{not}(\text{if } P \text{ then } Q)=P \ \textbf{and}\ \text{not }Q$$

The negation is **not** another implication: it says the hypothesis holds **but** the conclusion fails.

[not("if $x<0$ then $x^3<0$") $=$ "$x<0$ **and** $x^3\ge0$"]{.eg}
:::

::::

## Traps, and the order of quantifiers

:::: {.fs-grid}

::: {.fs-card}
### "not all" ≠ "none"

The negation of **"all are $Y$"** is **"at least one is not $Y$"** (a *there exists*) — **never**
"none is $Y$".

$$\text{not(all } Y)=\text{some is not } Y \neq \text{no } Y$$

["no multiple of $4$ is even" is far stronger — and false; the real negation needs just **one** exception]{.eg}
:::

::: {.fs-card}
### Order of quantifiers

Swapping **for all** and **there exists** changes the meaning:

$$\underbrace{\text{for all } m,\ \text{there exists } n,\ n>m}_{\textbf{true}}$$
$$\underbrace{\text{there exists } n,\ \text{for all } m,\ n>m}_{\textbf{false}}$$

[first: $n$ is picked **after** $m$, so it may depend on it; second: one $n$ must beat **every** $m$]{.eg}
:::

::: {.fs-card}
### Where these show up (cross-exam)

Paper 2 **Arg3/Arg4** tests exactly this — usually as multiple choice: "which is the negation of…",
"which statement is true". Quantifier-order questions and De Morgan negations also appear on **MAT** and
**STEP** reasoning.
:::

## True or false? — test yourself

The Paper 2 quantifier questions come in two flavours: *is this quantified statement true?* and *is this
negation / logical rule correct?* Memorise the verdict on each; **the *False* ones are the traps.**

**A. Are these quantified statements true?**

| Statement | T / F ? |
|---|:--:|
| For all real $x$, $\;x^2+1>0$. | |
| For all integers $n$, $\;2n$ is even. | |
| For every integer $n$, $\;n^2\ge n$. | |
| For all real $x$, if $x>2$ then $x^2>4$. | |
| There exists a real $x$ such that $x^2=x$. | |
| There exists an integer that is prime and even. | |
| For all real $x$, $\;x^2>0$. | |
| There exists a real $x$ such that $x^2=-1$. | |
| There exists an integer $n$ such that $n^2=2$. | |

**B. Are these negations / logical rules correct?**

| Statement | T / F ? |
|---|:--:|
| The negation of "all cats are grey" is "some cat is not grey". | |
| The negation of "there exists $x$ with $P(x)$" is "for all $x$, not $P(x)$". | |
| $\text{not}(A \text{ and } B)$ is the same as $(\text{not }A)\text{ or }(\text{not }B)$. | |
| $\text{not}(A \text{ or } B)$ is the same as $(\text{not }A)\text{ and }(\text{not }B)$. | |
| The negation of "if $P$ then $Q$" is "$P$ and not $Q$". | |
| "for some" means the same as "there exists at least one". | |
| The negation of "all cats are grey" is "no cat is grey". | |
| $\text{not}(A \text{ and } B)$ is the same as $(\text{not }A)\text{ and }(\text{not }B)$. | |
| The negation of "if $P$ then $Q$" is "if $P$ then not $Q$". | |
| "for all $x$, there exists $y$" means the same as "there exists $y$, for all $x$". | |
| "not all $X$ are $Y$" is the same as "no $X$ is $Y$". | |

## Proofs of the "true or false?" facts

Decide each verdict above first, then open the key.

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" appearance="simple" icon=false}
## A. Are these quantified statements true? — answers & proofs
- $\forall$ real $x,\ x^2+1>0$ — **True**: $x^2\ge0$, so $x^2+1\ge1$.
- $\forall$ integers $n,\ 2n$ even — **True**: $2n=2\cdot n$.
- $\forall$ integer $n,\ n^2\ge n$ — **True**: $n^2-n=n(n-1)\ge0$ for every integer.
- $\forall$ real $x$, if $x>2$ then $x^2>4$ — **True**: $x>2>0\Rightarrow x^2>4$.
- $\exists$ real $x,\ x^2=x$ — **True**: $x=0$ (or $x=1$).
- $\exists$ integer that is prime and even — **True**: $2$.
- $\forall$ real $x,\ x^2>0$ — **False**: $x=0$ gives $x^2=0$.
- $\exists$ real $x,\ x^2=-1$ — **False**: a real square is $\ge0$.
- $\exists$ integer $n,\ n^2=2$ — **False**: $\sqrt2$ is not an integer.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" appearance="simple" icon=false}
## B. Are these negations / logical rules correct? — answers & proofs
- Negation of "all cats are grey" is "some cat is not grey" — **True**: $\lnot\forall = \exists\lnot$.
- Negation of "$\exists x$ with $P(x)$" is "$\forall x,\ \lnot P(x)$" — **True**: $\lnot\exists = \forall\lnot$.
- $\lnot(A\text{ and }B)=(\lnot A)\text{ or }(\lnot B)$ — **True**: De Morgan.
- $\lnot(A\text{ or }B)=(\lnot A)\text{ and }(\lnot B)$ — **True**: De Morgan.
- Negation of "if $P$ then $Q$" is "$P$ and not $Q$" — **True**.
- "for some" means "there exists at least one" — **True**.
- Negation of "all cats are grey" is "no cat is grey" — **False**: the negation needs just **one** non-grey cat, not every cat non-grey.
- $\lnot(A\text{ and }B)=(\lnot A)\text{ and }(\lnot B)$ — **False**: De Morgan turns *and* into **or**.
- Negation of "if $P$ then $Q$" is "if $P$ then not $Q$" — **False**: it is "$P$ and not $Q$", not another implication.
- "$\forall x,\ \exists y$" means "$\exists y,\ \forall x$" — **False**: swapping the quantifiers changes the meaning.
- "not all $X$ are $Y$" is "no $X$ is $Y$" — **False**: "not all" needs one exception; "none" needs every case to fail.
:::

## Notes

### For all, there exists — and "for some"

**"for all"** asserts a property of *every* object; a single exception makes it false. **"there
exists"** (the exam also says **"for some"** and **"for at least one"**, all meaning the same) asserts
that *at least one* object has the property; it is false only when *nothing* does. Keeping straight *what
makes each false* is half of this topic — because negation turns one into the other.

### The two negation rules

To negate a quantified statement, do **both** of these:

::: {.keyline}
1. **flip the quantifier** — "for all" ↔ "there exists"; &nbsp; 2. **negate the inside**.
:::

Change only one and the negation is wrong — the standard slip.

::: {.example}
[Example.]{.lbl} Negate: "For all real $x$, $\;x^3\ge0$."
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" appearance="simple" icon=false}
## Solution
Flip *for all* → *there exists*, and negate $x^3\ge0$ to $x^3<0$:

> **There exists a real $x$ such that $x^3<0$.** &nbsp;*(True — e.g. $x=-1$.)* $\;\blacksquare$
:::

::: {.workbox}

:::

### De Morgan — negating *and* and *or*

When the inside is a compound "$A$ **and** $B$" or "$A$ **or** $B$", negating it uses **De Morgan's
laws**: negation turns **and** into **or**, and **or** into **and**, negating each part:

::: {.keyline}
not($A$ and $B$) $=$ (not $A$) **or** (not $B$) &nbsp;&nbsp;·&nbsp;&nbsp; not($A$ or $B$) $=$ (not $A$) **and** (not $B$)
:::

The picture: to break "$A$ **and** $B$" you only need **one** of them to fail (hence *or*); to break "$A$
**or** $B$" you need **both** to fail (hence *and*).

::: {.example}
[Example.]{.lbl} Negate: "There exists an integer $n$ such that $n$ is odd **and** $n>100$."
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" appearance="simple" icon=false}
## Solution
Flip *there exists* → *for all*, then apply De Morgan to "odd **and** $>100$":

> **For all integers $n$, &nbsp; $n$ is even **or** $n\le100$.** $\;\blacksquare$

*Two moves at once: the quantifier flips, **and** the "and" inside becomes "or". Missing the De Morgan
swap — writing "even **and** $\le100$" — is the usual error.*
:::

::: {.workbox}

:::

### Negating an implication

An "if $P$ then $Q$" is broken only when $P$ is true but $Q$ fails. So its negation is **not** another
implication:

::: {.keyline}
not(if $P$ then $Q$) $=$ $P$ **and** (not $Q$).
:::

::: {.example}
[Example.]{.lbl} Negate: "For all real $x$, if $x<0$ then $x^3<0$."
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" appearance="simple" icon=false}
## Solution
Flip *for all* → *there exists*; negate the implication to "$x<0$ **and** $x^3\ge0$":

> **There exists a real $x$ such that $x<0$ and $x^3\ge0$.** &nbsp;*(False, but correctly formed.)*
> $\;\blacksquare$

*The negation keeps the hypothesis and denies the conclusion — never "if $x<0$ then $x^3\ge0$".*
:::

::: {.workbox}

:::

### "not all" is not "none"

A favourite trap. The negation of **"all multiples of $4$ are even"** is **"at least one multiple of $4$
is not even"** — a *there exists* needing a single exception. It is **not** "no multiple of $4$ is even",
which claims *every* one is odd — a much stronger (and here false) statement.

::: {.keyline}
not(all are $Y$) $=$ **some** is not $Y$ &nbsp; (one exception) &nbsp;≠&nbsp; **no** is $Y$ (all fail).
:::

### The order of quantifiers

This is the deep one. Two statements can use the **same words in a different order** and mean different
things — one true, one false. Compare, over the positive integers:

- **P:** *For all $m$, there exists $n$ such that $n>m$.*
- **Q:** *There exists $n$ such that for all $m$, $n>m$.*

In **P**, "for all $m$" comes first, so $n$ is chosen **after** $m$ and may **depend on** it: *given any
$m$, there is some larger $n$* — take $n=m+1$. **P is true.**

In **Q**, "there exists $n$" comes first, so **one** $n$ is fixed **before** $m$ and must beat **every**
$m$: *there is a largest positive integer.* No such $n$ exists — **Q is false.**

::: {.example}
[Example.]{.lbl} Write the negation of **Q**: "there exists $n$ such that for all $m$, $n>m$."
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" appearance="simple" icon=false}
## Solution
Flip **each** quantifier in turn and negate the inside ($n>m$ becomes $n\le m$):

> **For all $n$, there exists $m$ such that $n\le m$.** $\;\blacksquare$

*In words: for every integer there is one at least as large — which is true, matching the fact that Q was
false. When there are two quantifiers, negation flips **both**, in order.*
:::

::: {.workbox}

:::
